PROFE

A long marriage. Unexpected desire. And the extraordinary people who make an ordinary life impossible to forget.

Private agent-review concept · Not publicly released
The Novel

Their lives are not finished. Neither are their surprises.

Daniel and Claire Bennett have built a long, satisfying marriage. Their children are grown. The demanding careers are behind them. They know each other’s habits, silences and jokes—or think they do.

Then retirement begins to feel less like a finish line than an invitation. Daniel starts teaching English across the border in Tijuana, where students with uncertain futures give him new purpose. A beautiful young Venezuelan woman also awakens a part of him he thought had grown quiet.

Claire, meanwhile, finds herself drawn to a man who sees her not as a wife, mother or retired attorney but as a woman still capable of being wanted. Neither she nor Daniel is prepared for what these separate encounters reveal about the life they have made together.

Profe is a novel of later-life longing and loyalty, but also of newcomers who have already lived more stories than most of us can imagine. Their humor, resourcefulness, generosity and hopes are not a backdrop to Daniel and Claire’s marriage. They matter in their own right.

A visual introduction to the book

A marriage. Two temptations. A border.

Daniel crosses into Tijuana with a whiteboard and discovers people who need him—and a young woman whose attention unsettles him. Claire remains in San Diego, where an unexpected attraction begins to test her ideas about fidelity, independence and desire.

Their adventures are different, but they turn toward the same question: after decades of sharing a life, how much of yourself still belongs only to you?

There is tenderness here, and sex, and humor, and recklessness. There are also students who cannot afford the luxury of second chances. The book moves between those worlds without asking either one to stand for the other.

Profe is a work of fiction inspired by real experiences, relationships and places.

The other side of Profe

Desire still has a pulse. So does the world beyond their door.

What if the person who knows you best no longer knows everything about you?

Daniel

The beautiful distraction

A retired judge who thought he was going to teach English finds himself wanting to be useful, brave—and wanted. In Tijuana, Marisol challenges his confidence in the boundaries he has always trusted.

Claire

A door she never meant to open

Claire is nobody’s neglected wife. Smart, accomplished and alive to her own appetites, she discovers that being desired by Darius can be intoxicating even when she knows precisely what she stands to lose.

Together

Not teenagers again. Something better.

Years of marriage have not used up their capacity for surprise. Beneath flirtation and betrayal lies a love that can still make room for laughter, physical tenderness and an entirely new kind of honesty.

What if the most surprising affair of your later years is with the person you married?

This is an adult novel about two people still learning what it means to want, to be wanted, and to choose each other. The sensuality is part of the story—not an apology for their ages and not a joke about them.

Inside the classroom

They came for English. They brought entire lives.

A barber dreaming of a place to open his shop. Haitian girls hoping to join family in Boston. A father trying to build something permanent after losing nearly everything. Someone who understood a letter, then helped the next person understand theirs.

Daniel meets people who have endured detention, separation, dangerous travel and the long uncertainty of waiting for permission to stay. But they are not defined by the worst thing that happened to them. They tease one another, work, cook, argue about the future, fall in love, and look after children who just want to play.

Some days the classroom was grammar and new words. Other days there was food, shared jokes—and there was dancing. Outside, children found room for a ball, a game, a little competition, the same noisy pleasures children find wherever they live.

These friendships are the reason Profe is not simply a story about a retired judge who crosses the border. The students change him, and they stay with the reader long after the lessons end. Their fictional lives are inspired by real encounters, but identifying details and circumstances have been changed.

The real places behind the fiction

The world that changed everything.

For approximately five years, Doug Cooper crossed into Tijuana to teach English to immigrants. The photographs and video below come from that world—not a film set, not stock photography.

When the danger comes closer

Daniel keeps going back. The risks stop being abstract.

Warnings become encounters. The classroom is no longer sealed off from the violence around it. What begins as a few mornings teaching English draws Daniel deeper into a city where danger is never far away. When violence finally reaches him, the life he has come to love in Tijuana is suddenly beyond his reach.

The classroom

The whiteboard was real, too.

A room, a board crowded with English and Spanish, and people learning the words they hoped might change their lives.

The novel is fiction, but its atmosphere grew from actual lessons, conversations and friendships. Some of those friendships continue today in Mexico and across the United States.

The border

Twenty minutes away. A different world.

The fence, the people waiting, the classrooms and the ordinary streets beyond the crossing shaped the novel’s sense of place.

Profe explores how closely two worlds can stand—and how far apart a single decision can leave them.

One of the real people behind the fiction

Maria was already there.

Maria, surrounded by children and families. Review-only photograph; not cleared for promotional use.

The real Maria created the space where many of these friendships began: a crowded office where someone was always making room for one more person.

Maria helped make the English lessons possible. The office was more than a place to practice verbs. People came with questions, children, empty stomachs, notices they did not know how to read, and the hope that someone would listen. Some days there were hot dogs. Other days quesadillas or chicken tacos, tortillas and soft drinks. A lesson might begin with a whiteboard and end with an entirely different problem.

Maria has also brought water to people waiting at the border. She works babysitting and cleaning jobs to help pay office rent and often uses her own money to buy food. Recently, she told Doug she had considered closing the office: keeping it running is exhausting. But somebody else always needs help, and she keeps showing up.

When Doug recently shared passages from Profe with her over lunch, Maria laughed at the scenes and was surprised at how much he remembered. They remain in touch. The fictional Maria Galleta honors the generosity and determination of the real Maria, without claiming that every scene in the novel happened exactly as written.

The classroom existed because someone kept opening the door.

Maria has said she is comfortable being acknowledged as an inspiration. A named portrait, exact quotations, and additional publicity will be added only with her approval of their specific use.

Inside the classroom

What a whiteboard cannot show

Language

At the most ordinary level, people wanted words for work, school, neighbors, families and the everyday business of making a life in a new place.

Belonging

A class could bring together people from different countries and backgrounds, each at a different point in a journey. They shared more than grammar.

Friendship

Some former students are now in Boston, Texas, Colorado and elsewhere; others remain in Tijuana. Several friendships continued long after the lessons ended.

Those encounters helped inspire fictional characters including Lucien, the Haitian families and Wilfred. The novel deliberately changes identifying details and combines experiences. The real people retain ownership of their own stories.

The fiction portfolio

One finished world.
More lives waiting to be lived.

Profe is the lead novel. Beyond it, Doug Cooper is developing character-driven fiction about reinvention, desire, and the surprises that change the stories people tell themselves. Here is a look at two novels in development.

Companion novel in development · Cover concept

Claire After

After the death of her husband Daniel, Claire Bennett is finally free to discover what comes next. But a young woman's startling claim about Daniel draws her into an investigation where love, memory and even photographic evidence cannot be taken at face value. A witty, sensual novel of secrets, second chances and an appetite for life that refuses to fade.

Standalone novel in development · Cover concept

A Theory of Wanting

Nora can explain molecular biology but knows remarkably little about desire. An unexpected kiss leaves her questioning everything, and she does what any good scientist might do: she forms hypotheses. Dating disasters, surprising discoveries and irreverent emails with Leila turn her research into a funny, intimate adventure in learning what—and whom—she truly wants.

Three distinct stories. A shared interest in complicated people, emotional surprises, and the possibility of becoming someone new.

About the author

Doug Cooper

The story began long before the novel: in Tijuana classrooms, at the border crossing, and in friendships that outlasted the lessons.

Cooper is a San Diego-based writer and longtime volunteer teacher. His original photographs and videos document classrooms, everyday encounters and friendships that helped inspire the novel.

Doug Cooper with one of his classes outside in Tijuana — a real moment from the world that inspired Profe.

The author

How the novel began

Doug Cooper crossed the San Ysidro border to teach English in Tijuana over approximately five years. In the classroom, he found conversation, humor, generosity and friendships that expanded far beyond a weekly lesson.

He lives in San Diego and has spent years participating in service and community work involving immigrants, homelessness and food distribution. Profe is his first novel. The book also draws on a fascination with the possibilities of later life: adventure, tenderness, temptation, reinvention and the work we choose when no one is telling us what to do.

His independently produced Hidden Paths Immigration video archive has documented personal encounters, teaching and immigration stories. In October 2026, the associated channel had 1,062 followers and 1,393 likes. A selected collection of relevant original footage is presented on this page.

The next conversation

For readers, book clubs and publishing partners

What does fidelity mean after forty years? Can desire deepen with age? How do we keep growing without abandoning the people who grew beside us? And whose future does a border allow us to imagine?

These questions make Profe a book-club novel as much as a border novel. Its two intertwined stories create space for conversations about marriage, sexual confidence, reinvention, grief and the rights of people struggling to begin again. The author’s real-life relationships in Tijuana also offer opportunities for readings, interviews and community conversations.

One day, Doug hopes the attention surrounding the book might also help sustain the real Maria's office. Any effort to support it would be arranged separately, transparently and with Maria's participation.
